summary:
**Division P — Tax-Related Provisions** (H.R. 2029, 114th Congress) does not fund a department. It changes the tax code. No appropriation totals or dollar amounts appear in the text.

## Overview

This division is a package of tax-law changes attached to the omnibus, not a spending bill for an agency. It delays two Affordable Care Act taxes on expensive job-based health plans and on health insurers, and it extends and gradually phases down tax credits for wind and solar energy. It also gives independent oil refiners a temporary, limited change in how transportation costs are counted for a domestic-production tax deduction.

## Total Spending

**No appropriation amount is in this division.** It does not appropriate money. It amends the Internal Revenue Code and the Affordable Care Act. Any effect on the federal budget would be through higher or lower tax collections, and this text does not estimate that revenue impact.

## Key Funding Areas

There are no funded programs or line-item appropriations. The notable items are tax changes:

- **“Cadillac tax” delay (Sec. 101)**: No dollar figure — pushes back the excise tax on high-cost employer health coverage. The law’s start year reference is changed from 2017 to 2019, so the tax is delayed by two years (from 2018 to 2020).
- **Cadillac tax made deductible (Sec. 102)**: No dollar figure — when the tax eventually applies, the payer may deduct it. A general rule that bars deductions for certain taxes is turned off for this tax.
- **Health-insurer fee moratorium (Sec. 201)**: No dollar figure — the annual fee on health insurance providers does not apply for calendar year 2017. It applies for 2014–2016 and again for years after 2017.
- **Wind production tax credit (Sec. 301)**: No dollar figure — the “begin construction” deadline moves from January 1, 2015, to January 1, 2020. The credit is then cut by 20% for projects started in 2017, 40% in 2018, and 60% in 2019.
- **Wind investment-credit election (Sec. 302)**: No dollar figure — the option to take an investment credit instead of the production credit is extended on the same schedule, with the same phase-down for wind.
- **Business solar credit (Sec. 303)**: No dollar figure — the higher solar investment credit is extended for property whose construction begins before January 1, 2022. The rate is 26% for construction starting in 2020 and 22% in 2021. Property not placed in service before January 1, 2024, gets 10%.
- **Homeowner solar credit (Sec. 304)**: No dollar figure — the residential credit for solar electric systems and solar water heaters runs through 2021: 30% for property placed in service in 2017–2019, 26% in 2020, and 22% in 2021.
- **Independent refiners (Sec. 305)**: No dollar figure — for refiners that are not major integrated oil companies, only 25% of oil transportation costs are counted against certain domestic-production receipts when figuring the section 199 deduction. Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2015, and ends after 2021.

## Notable Provisions

- The Cadillac-tax delay is a straight date change in the Affordable Care Act (2017 → 2019), plus a technical wording fix on how the dollar limit is determined.
- A Government Accountability Office study is due within 18 months on whether the Blue Cross/Blue Shield standard option in the federal employee health plan is a good benchmark for age and gender adjustments to the Cadillac-tax limit, and whether a better benchmark exists. GAO must consult state insurance regulators and report to the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees.
- The insurer-fee pause is one calendar year only (2017), not a repeal.
- Wind and solar credits are extended but set on a declining schedule rather than made permanent. Wind steps down over 2017–2019; commercial solar steps down in 2020–2021, with a placed-in-service cutoff of January 1, 2024; residential solar steps down and ends after 2021.
- Wind and the related investment-credit election changes are effective January 1, 2015 (retroactive to the prior deadline). The business solar changes take effect on enactment. The residential solar changes take effect January 1, 2017.
- The refiner provision is limited to independent refiners, covers transportation costs only, and expires for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021.

## Who Benefits

- Employers that offer expensive health plans, and the workers in those plans, get a two-year reprieve from the high-cost-plan excise tax. Making the tax deductible later reduces its net cost to whoever pays it.
- Health insurance companies skip the annual provider fee for 2017.
- Wind developers and investors get more time to start projects and a known phase-down instead of an immediate cutoff.
- Businesses that install solar, and homeowners who buy solar electric systems or solar water heaters, get extended credits at declining rates.
- Independent oil refiners (not the largest integrated oil companies) get a temporary rule that can increase the domestic-production deduction by counting only a quarter of oil transportation costs in that calculation.
- The study benefits Congress, which receives a GAO report; it does not itself change anyone’s taxes.

## Plain English Summary

This part of the bill doesn’t hand any agency a budget. It tweaks taxes. It puts off, for two years, a tax on the most expensive employer health plans, and it lets insurers skip a special yearly fee for 2017. It also keeps tax breaks for wind and solar going longer, but shrinks them over time so they don’t stay at the full rate forever. Homeowners who put in solar get a credit that stays at 30% for a few more years, then drops to 26% and 22% before it ends. Smaller, independent oil refiners get a short-term break in how shipping costs count toward a manufacturing-style tax deduction. The bill itself doesn’t say how many dollars any of this costs or saves the Treasury.

titles.header: HIGH COST EMPLOYER-SPONSORED HEALTH COVERAGE EXCISE TAX PROVISIONS
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

This title does not appropriate funds. It changes the Affordable Care Act’s excise tax on high-cost employer-sponsored health coverage (the “Cadillac tax,” IRC §4980I). It delays the tax’s start date, makes the tax deductible, and orders a Government Accountability Office (GAO) study of age and gender adjustment benchmarks.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Appropriations | None | This title contains no spending authority or dollar amounts. |
| Sec. 101 — Delay of excise tax | No appropriation | Moves the effective year of the high-cost coverage excise tax from 2017 to 2019 (PPACA §§9001(c) and 10901(c), as amended). |
| Sec. 102 — Deductibility | No appropriation | Provides that IRC §275(a)(6) does not apply to the §4980I tax, so the tax is deductible. |
| Sec. 103 — GAO study | No appropriation | Requires a Comptroller General report within 18 months of enactment. |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 101 — Delay.** Strikes “2017” and inserts “2019” in the ACA provisions that set the tax’s effective date, postponing the tax by two years. A conforming amendment updates IRC §4980I(b)(3)(C)(v) wording from “as in effect” / “as so in effect” to “as determined for” / “as so determined.”
- **Sec. 102 — Deductibility.** Rewrites IRC §4980I(f)(10) so the general rule barring deduction of certain taxes does not apply to this excise tax.
- **Sec. 103 — Benchmark study.** Directs the Comptroller General, in consultation with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, to report to the Senate Finance Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee on whether the Blue Cross/Blue Shield standard benefit option under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Plan is a suitable benchmark for age and gender adjustments to the tax’s dollar limit, and to recommend any better benchmarks. Deadline: 18 months after enactment. No new tax program is created.

## Plain English

This title pushes back the start of the tax on expensive job-based health plans by two years, lets employers deduct that tax, and asks GAO to review how the tax is adjusted for age and gender.

titles.header: ANNUAL FEE ON HEALTH INSURANCE PROVIDERS
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

Title II of Division P does not appropriate funds. It amends section 9010 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act to suspend the annual fee on health insurance providers for calendar year 2017. The fee remains in effect for 2014–2016 and resumes for calendar years beginning after December 31, 2017.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Annual fee on health insurance providers (ACA §9010) | No dollar amount in this title | One-year moratorium for calendar year 2017; fee applies for 2014–2016 and again starting in 2018 |

This title contains no appropriations or specified dollar amounts. It only changes the effective dates of an existing industry fee.

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 201 — Moratorium on annual fee on health insurance providers.** Rewrites ACA §9010(j) so the fee applies to calendar years beginning after December 31, 2013, and ending before January 1, 2017, and to calendar years beginning after December 31, 2017. That leaves calendar year 2017 uncovered—a one-year suspension, not a repeal. No new program is created.

## Plain English

Health insurers get a one-year break from the federal annual fee in 2017, and the fee comes back in 2018.

## Title Summary

Title III amends the Internal Revenue Code; it does not appropriate funds. It extends and phases out the production and investment tax credits for wind facilities (secs. 45 and 48), extends and phases out the business and residential solar energy credits (secs. 48 and 25D), and temporarily changes how independent refiners allocate oil transportation costs under the section 199 domestic production deduction.

## Spending Breakdown

No dollar amounts are appropriated in this title. The figures below are statutory credit rates and allocation percentages, not spending.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Wind production tax credit (sec. 301) | Construction start deadline extended to Jan. 1, 2020; credit reduced 20% / 40% / 60% for starts in 2017 / 2018 / 2019 | Extends and phases out the sec. 45 credit for electricity from wind |
| Wind investment-credit election (sec. 302) | Same Jan. 1, 2020 deadline and 20% / 40% / 60% reductions | Lets wind facilities elect the sec. 48 investment credit on the same phaseout |
| Business solar energy credit (sec. 303) | 26% if construction begins in 2020; 22% if it begins in 2021; 10% if not placed in service before Jan. 1, 2024 | Extends the sec. 48 solar credit for construction beginning before Jan. 1, 2022, then steps it down |
| Residential solar electric and solar water heating credits (sec. 304) | 30% if placed in service 2017–2019; 26% in 2020; 22% in 2021; expires after Dec. 31, 2021 | Extends and phases out the sec. 25D homeowner credits for those two property types |
| Independent refiners’ transportation costs (sec. 305) | 25% of otherwise allocable oil transportation costs count against oil-related qualified production activities income; ends for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2021 | Lowers the cost allocation used in the sec. 199 deduction for refiners that are not major integrated oil companies |

## Notable Sections

- **Secs. 301–302:** Multi-year wind credit extension with a built-in phaseout tied to when construction begins (not a new program). Effective Jan. 1, 2015.
- **Secs. 303–304:** Parallel solar extensions. Business solar can fall to a permanent-style 10% rate if a project is not placed in service before 2024; residential solar electric and water-heating credits end after 2021. Business changes take effect on enactment; residential changes take effect Jan. 1, 2017.
- **Sec. 305:** A targeted, temporary tax benefit for independent refiners only (major integrated oil companies are excluded). It does not create a spending program. Applies to tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2015, and terminates after 2021.

## Plain English

This title keeps federal tax credits for wind and solar projects in place for several more years, then gradually shrinks them, and gives independent oil refiners a temporary break in how transportation costs reduce a production tax deduction.
